opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting direction, and I'd frame it around one basic asymmetry: for many problems, it's much easier to verify an answer than to generate one. If I give you a math proof or a piece of code, checking whether it's correct, or at least spotting obvious mistakes, is often a simpler task than writing it from scratch. So if you have one model that's decent at judging, you can use it as a learning signal for another model that's trying to generate. That's essentially what's happening when people use a language model as a reward model or a critic in reinforcement learning.

A lot of my own thinking comes from energy-based models. You can view the evaluator as learning an energy function, a score over the space of possible answers that says how compatible a response is with the question. Generation then becomes a kind of optimization: you search for responses that the evaluator scores highly. Reinforcement learning with a model-based judge is one way to amortize that search, so the generator learns to directly produce answers the verifier likes, instead of sampling many candidates and filtering them at test time.

This also connects to our work on multi-agent debate. There we had multiple instances of a language model propose answers, read each other's reasoning, and critique and revise. We found that factuality and reasoning both improved, because each model was effectively evaluating the others. That's a kind of self-supervision you get without any human labels, and you can distill those improved answers back into a single model.

That said, I think there are real caveats. The biggest is reward hacking. If the evaluator is just another neural network, the generator will eventually find its blind spots. It learns to produce answers that look convincing, are confidently written, or are longer, rather than answers that are actually correct. And if the two models share the same pretraining data and the same biases, the evaluator may systematically miss the same errors the generator makes. You can end up in an echo chamber.

So I think the approach works best when the evaluator has some kind of genuine advantage over the generator. That could be access to tools, like running code or checking against retrieved facts. It could be decomposition, scoring individual reasoning steps rather than only the final answer. Or it could be composition, combining several independent judges so that no single one's blind spot dominates. Grounding the evaluation in something external, like execution, simulation, or the physical world, matters a lot. Without that, you're mostly redistributing knowledge the models already have rather than creating new knowledge.

Longer term, I think this points toward systems that aren't just a single feed-forward generator. Instead they have an internal notion of verification and can spend more computation thinking, checking, and refining when a problem is hard. Using one model to evaluate another is an early, somewhat external version of that idea, and I expect those generate-and-verify loops to become more tightly integrated into how these models reason.

r001.rationale: The response mentions checking correctness, evaluating reasoning, and scoring reasoning steps, but it does not clearly distinguish judging whether an answer matches a ground-truth answer from judging whether its reasoning makes sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about it is that it's really a question of what signal you actually have access to. In a lot of domains, there's no ground truth reward sitting there for you. If you're training a model to write a good proof, or a good essay, or to plan a multi-step task in some environment, there's no simple function that says "this was a seven out of ten." So what people do is they take another language model, often a stronger one or just a copy of the same model, and they ask it to judge: is this response correct, is it helpful, does it follow the constraints. And then you use that judgment as the reward signal for RL.

And I think the reason it works at all is this asymmetry between verification and generation. It's often much easier to look at a candidate answer and check whether it's right than it is to produce the answer from scratch. So even if the judge model couldn't solve the problem itself, it can often tell when something has gone wrong. That gap is what you're exploiting. The policy proposes, the critic verifies, and over time the policy gets pulled toward the things the verifier approves of.

But I'd say I'm fairly cautious about it, because the obvious failure mode is reward hacking. The policy isn't optimizing for being correct, it's optimizing for whatever the judge rewards, and those are only the same thing if the judge is actually robust. In practice you see the policy learn to write longer, more confident-sounding responses, or to adopt a particular style the judge happens to like, or to say the right keywords without actually doing the reasoning. The judge has blind spots, and RL is very good at finding them. And the more you optimize, the more you drift into the regime where the judge's errors dominate.

So a lot of my thinking has been about how you make the verification side more grounded. One direction is to decompose things, so instead of one holistic score you have the judge check individual steps or individual constraints, and errors are more localized and harder to fake. Another is to connect the judge to something external where you can, like actually executing code, or checking against a simulator, or comparing against a world model of what should happen. And a third is to treat it more like a generative process, where the judge is sampling many candidate critiques and you aggregate them, rather than trusting a single forward pass. All of those are really about the same thing, which is making the reward closer to something that's actually true about the world rather than something that's just an opinion of another model.

So I'd say it's a very useful tool, and honestly for a lot of open-ended tasks it's the only scalable option we have right now. But I think of it as a bridge. The long-term thing you want is reward that comes from the environment, from consequences, from whether the thing actually worked. And model-based judges are a way to approximate that until you can get there.

r001.rationale: The response mentions judging whether an answer is correct and checking individual steps, but it does not clearly distinguish matching a ground-truth answer from assessing whether the reasoning makes sense.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as using one model to provide a reward signal for another. You generate a response, and then you ask the evaluator model, “How good is this response? Does it satisfy the request?” You can use that feedback to train the model that produced it, instead of having a human judge every example.

The appeal is that evaluating an answer can sometimes be easier than generating it. A model might recognize a mistake in a proposed solution even when it couldn’t produce the correct solution on its own. So there’s an opportunity to get useful supervision that way.

But the evaluator is still imperfect. If you optimize too aggressively against its judgments, you can end up with responses that look good to that evaluator without actually being more correct or useful. So the central question is how well that reward signal captures what you really want, and how you check that improvements carry over beyond the evaluator itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes judging whether an answer is good, satisfies the request, or contains a mistake, but does not distinguish checking it against a ground-truth answer from assessing whether its reasoning makes sense.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that reinforcement learning needs some signal of what constitutes a good response. You can get that from humans, but collecting human feedback for every response is expensive. So one approach is to have another language model look at the response and judge whether it satisfies certain criteria, or compare two responses and say which one is better. That judgment then becomes a reward signal for training.

The important question is how reliable that judge is. It can be useful even if it can’t generate the best answer itself—recognizing a good solution can be easier than producing one. But it can also make mistakes, and the model being trained can learn to exploit those mistakes. It might learn to produce something that sounds convincing to the evaluator without actually being correct.

So I think it’s a useful way to scale feedback, but you want to ground that feedback in things you can check independently whenever possible. If it’s code, for example, you can execute it and test whether it works. The stronger that connection to an actual outcome, the more confidence you can have in the training signal.

r001.rationale: The response describes an evaluator judging criteria or comparing answers, but does not distinguish checking a generated answer against a ground-truth answer from assessing whether its reasoning makes sense.
